newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Christian Democrat Koller elected Swiss president.
newsitem.headline: Christian Democrat Koller elected Swiss president.

text.p: Switzerland's parliament elected Justice Minister Arnold Koller to a one-year term as the country's president on Friday, putting him in the hot seat for what could be a turbulent period for international relations.

Koller, 63, a Christian Democrat, takes up the largely ceremonial position in 1997. He was also president in 1990 under Switzerland's leadership system that rotates the job according to length of service in the seven-member cabinet.
He received 171 of 192 valid votes cast to succeed Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz. He remains justice minister in the four-party coalition that has governed since 1959.

Koller, a lawyer and professor who specialises in commercial law, has been a cabinet member since 1987. His austere political style fits in well with the ministry's detailed work on legislation and his handling of sensitive social issues.
His crowning achievement would be adoption of a new constitution, after 30 years of effort, by the 150th anniversary in 1998 of Switzerland's becoming a modern federal state.
Koller takes the helm at a time of unprecedented foreign criticism of Switzerland that will test his diplomatic skills.

Driven by documents now emerging from wartime archives, Jewish groups and prominent U.S. legislators have slammed Switzerland's business ties with Nazi Germany and accused Swiss banks of sitting on the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims.
Swiss banks deny the charges but have agreed to work with Jewish groups to probe the allegations.
Critics have also alleged Berne used the dormant wealth of Hitler's victims to help compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by post-war communist regimes in Eastern Europe.

The Swiss parliament is set to give final approval next week to forming a panel of historians empowered to lift strict banking secrecy in some cases and conduct a sweeping review of neutral Switzerland's role as a wartime financial centre.
